faqs.answer: 7 g of powder-fine coffee to 70 ml of water at 1:10. That is about one heaped teaspoon of coffee per small cup.
faqs.question: How much coffee for one cup of Turkish coffee?

faqs.answer: To a powder, finer than espresso, like flour. A burr grinder on its finest setting can do it, or buy coffee ground for Turkish.
faqs.question: How fine should Turkish coffee be ground?

faqs.answer: Once, at the start, to wet the grounds. After that, leave it alone. Stirring breaks the foam, and the foam is the best part of the cup.
faqs.question: Do you stir Turkish coffee?

faqs.answer: No. Heat it slowly and take it off just before it boils, when the foam rises to the rim. Boiling breaks the foam and makes the coffee taste burnt.
faqs.question: Should Turkish coffee boil?

faqs.answer: They settle to the bottom of the cup. Drink slowly and stop before the last sip, which is mostly grounds.
faqs.question: Do you drink the grounds in Turkish coffee?

felicityNote: Turkish coffee is the slowest cup I make and the smallest, and somehow the one I look forward to most. Seven grams, cold water, low heat, patience.

howToSteps.name: Measure coffee and water
howToSteps.text: Use 7 g of powder-fine coffee and 70 ml of cold water per cup. Add sugar now if you want it.

howToSteps.name: Stir once
howToSteps.text: Put the coffee, water, and sugar in the cezve and stir once until the coffee is wet. Do not stir again.

howToSteps.name: Heat slowly
howToSteps.text: Put the cezve on the lowest heat. The coffee will foam as it warms. Watch it closely: it goes from foaming to boiling in seconds.

howToSteps.name: Take it off before it boils
howToSteps.text: When the foam rises to the rim, lift the cezve off the heat. Pour slowly into small cups, sharing the foam between them. Wait a minute for the grounds to settle before drinking.

lede: Turkish coffee starts at 1:10, one gram of coffee for every 10 grams of water. That is 7 g of powder-fine coffee to 70 ml of water for one small cup.

title: Turkish Coffee to Water Ratio Guide
tutorial: Turkish coffee uses the most coffee for its size of any method here: 1:10, which is 7 g of coffee to 70 ml of water for one small cup. Nothing is filtered out, so the fine grounds stay in the cup, and the ratio has to carry the whole drink.

The published range is 1:9 to 1:12. At 1:9 the cup is thick and intense, which is how many Turkish coffee drinkers like it. At 1:12 it is lighter and easier for a first try. Start at 1:10 and move from there.

Grind finer than espresso, to a powder. The coffee should feel like flour between your fingers. A blade grinder will not get there; you need a burr grinder on its finest setting, or coffee ground for Turkish at the shop. Pre-ground Turkish coffee from a Middle Eastern grocer is a good shortcut.

Start with cold water and heat it slowly on the lowest flame. Stir once, at the start, and then leave it alone. The coffee foams as it heats, and you take it off just before it boils, when the foam rises to the rim. Let it boil and the foam breaks and the coffee tastes burnt.

Sugar goes in at the start, not at the end, because you cannot stir the finished cup without breaking the foam. The traditional sweetnesses are plain, a little sweet, and sweet. Add the sugar with the coffee and cold water, stir once, and heat it all together.
